newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - Forward sales help S.Africa's gold mines.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Forward sales help S.Africa's gold mines.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

South Africa's gold mining industry was hit by the double whammy in the first quarter of 1997 of the average dollar gold price falling from $376.5 to $351.3 an ounce and the rand strengthening from an average 4.64 to 4.52 rands to the U.S. dollar.
With no alleviation in terms of average grades and a further 4.6 percent increase in rand working costs per unit of gold produced, the impact on working profits was little short of disastrous.
Working profit for the Chamber of Mines members of the industry fell sharply by 46 percent from 1.474 billion rand in the last quarter to 795 million rand.
Of the 27 reporting producers seven suffered working losses and they represented 12 percent of the total production.
However, if capital expenditure is taken into account there were altogether 11 producers showing overall financial loss and they represented 21 percent of total production.

One of the mitigating factors, however, turned out to be the handsome contribution to working revenues from forward selling. Instead of the rand average gold price in the quarter of 1,587 rand, the gold producers actually realised 1,627 rand an ounce.
This additional 40 rand effectively added 143 million rand to gross working revenues and to the working profits. In its absence the drop of working profits would have been as much as 56 percent.
On balance forward sales have had a stabilising effect on the industry, reducing the severity of sharp falls in price and dampening sharp increases.

Oddly enough the average market price in rand terms and the average price realised by the industry has worked out to be almost identical over the years but, of course, with slightly less variability in the latter.
The advantage of stabilising the realised price in a downturn is nevertheless evident.
Measures are already being mooted for retrenchment of workers as a result of the poor quarter and, clearly, these would be that much worse had it not been for the forward sales hedging.

The working profit, when reduced to dollar terms, gives a dismal picture and shows that the industry is a diminishing force. Ten years ago the quarterly working profit of the industry was of the order of $800 million.

This has been reduced to a quarterly average of $290 million in 1996 and to $318 million in the 1996 December quarter, in particular. It has plunged a further 45 percent in this last March quarter to $176 million.

Conversion of the various financial attributes of the industry to dollar terms has thrown up an interesting result, which could serve as a possible alternative to the purchasing power parity principle as a means of determining the "correct" value of the exchange rate as assessed economically.

The working cost of producing an ounce of gold metal when expressed in dollar terms turns out to be fairly constant at about $300. This provides a golden constant, which corresponds to the notion that over a limited time period the real costs of mining a metal remain much the same.
Actually, in this case the trend line in the scatter diagram of dollar working costs shows a small upward trend, effectively of 33 U.S. cents a quarter.

The theoretical or trend line value for the first quarter of 1997 is $302.1. This suggests that with the actual rand value of unit working costs at 1,410.9 rand, the "economically correct" value of the rand exchange rate averaged over the quarter was 4.67.
The actual exchange rate averaged over the quarter was 4.52, which indicates the degree of overvaluation of the rand in the quarter and its dampening effect on the economy.

Lord Keynes concluded that the Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) principle worked passably well in practice, although there are serious difficulties with the theory. That was in the context of the determination of exchange rates between comparable developed countries.
Further difficulties arise, particularily in a case like South Africa, where there is a dominance of primary exports, innate productivity problems and prices given on international markets.
It is not simplistically a matter of achieving parity for MacDonald's hamburgers.
The actual exchange rate is still a matter of what market determines it to be as influenced by the myriad of current and capital account transactions between South Africa and the rest of the world.

But this gold cost standard will provide a means of assessing the economic overvaluation or undervaluation of of the currency independent of the PPP principle and the difficulties about the appropriate starting point for applying it.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
